questions.q: In the Mulliken–Barker test, what does nitrobenzene give when warmed with zinc dust and aqueous NH₄Cl?
questions.explain: The almost neutral Zn/NH₄Cl mixture stops the four-electron reduction at C₆H₅NHOH. Aniline would need an acidic reducing medium such as Sn/HCl.

questions.q: Why is Sn/HCl not used in place of Zn/NH₄Cl for the reduction step of the Mulliken–Barker test?
options: Sn/HCl reduces the nitro group all the way to the amine, and amines do not reduce Tollens' reagent
Sn/HCl does not reduce aromatic nitro compounds
Sn/HCl precipitates silver chloride with Tollens' reagent, giving a false positive
Sn/HCl gives a hydroxylamine that is too stable to be oxidised
questions.explain: The test works only because the neutral medium halts reduction at R–NHOH, a reducing agent. In acid the product is R–NH₂, which leaves Tollens' reagent unchanged.

questions.q: A compound gives no silver with Tollens' reagent, but gives a grey-black silver precipitate after being boiled with Zn dust/NH₄Cl and filtered. The compound could be:
questions.explain: Aliphatic nitro compounds are also reduced to R–NHOH, which reduces Tollens' reagent. Benzaldehyde gives silver even before reduction, aniline never does, and nitrobenzoic acids often give a false negative.

questions.q: In the second step of the Mulliken–Barker test, N-phenylhydroxylamine reduces Tollens' reagent. Into what is it converted?
questions.explain: The hydroxylamine is oxidised to the nitroso compound C₆H₅NO while Ag⁺ is reduced to silver. 4-Aminophenol is the Bamberger product formed if the hydroxylamine stands in acid, which is why the filtrate is tested promptly.
